title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 25: Estrada v. Escritor: Religious Freedom as a Defense in Concubinage
keywords: Watch Tower and Bible Tract Society
Articles 334 and 349 of the Revised Penal Code
primary_topics: Chapter 25 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of Estrada v. Escritor, in which the Court found a court interpreter who lived with a man not her husband not administratively liable, holding that under the benevolent neutrality/accommodation reading of the religion clauses she had made out a case for exemption based on her fundamental right to freedom of religion.

The doctrinal core of the case: the choice between strict neutrality/strict separation and benevolent neutrality as the framework for construing the religion clauses, and the application of the three-step compelling-state-interest test to a Free Exercise claim.

The evidentiary turning point: the solicitor general conceded the sincerity and centrality of Escritor's belief, which shifted the burden to the government to show a compelling secular objective and the least intrusive means -- a burden it wholly failed to discharge.

The two Dissents -- Justice Carpio's (joined by the Chief Justice and Justices Morales and Callejo), arguing that Smith had already overturned the compelling-state-interest test and that the majority condoned a crime; and Justice Ynares-Santiago's, insisting the issue was legal, not religious.
sub_topics: Alejandro Estrada's sworn Letter-Complaint of July 27, 2000 asked Judge Jose F. Caoibes Jr. of the Las Pinas RTC to investigate court interpreter Soledad Escritor for living in with a man not her husband, an act he believed tarnished the image of the court.

Escritor was charged with 'disgraceful and immoral conduct' under the Revised Administrative Code; she testified that she had been a widow since 1998, that her live-in arrangement with Luciano Quilapio Jr. began more than twenty years earlier, and that her then-living husband was himself living with another woman.

As a member of Jehovah's Witnesses, she executed a 'Declaration of Pledging Faithfulness' on July 28, 1991, a form allowing abandoned spouses to enter marital relations with another and making the union moral and binding within the congregation, approved by the elders and recorded in the Watch Tower Central Office.

The declaration ceased to be valid once legal impediments were lifted; although Escritor's widowhood lifted hers in 1998, Quilapio was still not capacitated to remarry, so the couple remained in good standing and the congregation saw nothing immoral in the arrangement.

The first Decision of August 4, 2003 remanded the Complaint to the OCA and ordered the OSG to intervene to examine the sincerity and centrality of the belief, present evidence of the State's compelling interest, and show that the means chosen were the least restrictive of her religious freedom.

That first Decision became the law of the case, settling that benevolent neutrality or accommodation, whether mandatory or permissive, was the framework and that the compelling-state-interest test applied to the Free Exercise plea; only the factual basis remained to be resolved.

The Court surveyed the two opposing strains in U.S. jurisprudence: strict neutrality/strict separation anchored on the Jeffersonian 'wall of separation', its milder Everson version allowing only secular criteria for government action, and benevolent neutrality, which recognizes religion's role in public life and permits accommodation.

Three seminal Free Exercise cases were reviewed: Sherbert and Yoder, which subjected substantial burdens on religion to heightened scrutiny whether the burden was direct or indirect, and Smith, the peyote case, which abandoned strict scrutiny for neutral laws of general applicability in favor of the rational basis test.

Three kinds of accommodation were distinguished -- mandatory (constitutionally compelled, arising when all three conditions of the compelling interest test are met), permissive (the State may but need not accommodate), and prohibited (where establishment concerns prevail).

In the Philippine context the Court concluded that the accommodation approach is more pronounced here than in the United States; that the theory addresses the 'inadvertent burdensome effect' of facially neutral laws, criminal ones included; that accommodation protects minority religions from majoritarianism; that religious exemption from penal laws is not alien, Moslem polygamy having already been excepted from bigamy; and that the religion clauses, unlike other rights, are stated in absolute terms.

The compelling state interest test was set out as a three-step inquiry: has the statute burdened free exercise, is there a sufficiently compelling state interest, and did the State use the least intrusive means possible.

Applying it, the Court noted the solicitor general's categorical concession of sincerity and centrality, which shifted the burden to the government; the OSG offered no evidence of the gravest abuses endangering 'paramount interests' and none at all on least intrusive means, so the exemption was granted in this particular case and under these distinct circumstances.

Justice Carpio's Dissent argued that reliance on the obsolete Sherbert test was improper, that Smith should govern, that the State has a compelling interest in the highest standard of conduct from everyone connected with the dispensation of justice and in marriage and the family, and that the majority condoned a patent violation of the penal law on concubinage.

Carpio warned that the ruling could turn every religion into a separate republic and a haven for criminal conduct -- 'Today concubinage, tomorrow bigamy' -- and voted for suspension of six months and one day, liftable upon a manifestation that the cohabitation had ceased.

Justice Ynares-Santiago's Dissent held that the issue was legal, not religious: morality is measured by contemporary community standards, the acts were criminal under penal law, Escritor was charged in her capacity as a court employee and not as a Jehovah's Witness, and she should have been held administratively liable.

stances.claim: The framework for construing the Philippine religion clauses is benevolent neutrality or accommodation, and a claim of exemption under the Free Exercise Clause cannot simply be dismissed on the premise that the law in question is a general criminal law.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative doctrinal survey -- setting strict separation against benevolent neutrality, then showing that Philippine text and history give accommodation more leeway than American law does

stances.claim: Once the sincerity and centrality of the religious belief were conceded, the burden shifted to the government to show a compelling secular objective and the least intrusive means, and because the solicitor general offered no iota of evidence on either, Escritor's conjugal arrangement could not be penalized.
stances.rhetorical_move: burden-shifting applied step by step through the three-part compelling-state-interest test, with the government's silence treated as failure of proof

stances.claim: Mandatory accommodation is particularly necessary to protect the adherents of minority religions from the inevitable effects of majoritarianism -- ignorance, indifference and overt hostility -- and exemption from penal laws on account of religion is not an alien concept, Moslem polygamy having already been excepted from bigamy.
stances.rhetorical_move: minority-protection rationale reinforced by an existing statutory precedent for religious exemption from a penal law

stances.claim: In dissent, Justice Carpio argued that Smith had already overturned the compelling state interest test, that the State has a compelling interest in exacting the highest standard of conduct from everyone connected with the dispensation of justice, and that the majority effectively condoned a patent violation of the law on concubinage, so that 'today concubinage, tomorrow bigamy' would escape criminal sanction.
stances.rhetorical_move: slippery-slope warning attached to a claim that the majority relied on an obsolete test

stances.claim: In a separate Dissent, Justice Ynares-Santiago maintained that the issue was legal and not religious: morality is ascertained by contemporary community standards, the acts committed were criminal under penal law, and Escritor was charged in her capacity as a court employee rather than as a Jehovah's Witness.
stances.rhetorical_move: recharacterizing the question to remove it from the religion clauses altogether, backed by a plethora of cases on judiciary employees

notable_anecdotes: A court interpreter's twenty-year live-in arrangement became a disciplinary case when a private complainant wrote the presiding judge to say her conduct tarnished the image of the court and that keeping her employed would look like condoning it.
Escritor testified that when she joined the judiciary in 1999 she was already a widow, and that when her arrangement with Quilapio began her own husband was living with another woman.

The congregation's practice was strikingly formal: only baptized members in good standing could execute a 'Declaration of Pledging Faithfulness', the elders had to approve it, the marital status of the declarants and the spouses' adultery were investigated first, and the declaration was recorded in the Watch Tower Central Office.

The declarations expired by their own terms once legal impediments were lifted -- Escritor's husband died in 1998, but Quilapio remained married, so the couple's declarations remained valid and the congregation considered them in good standing.

The case was decided as much by what the government did not do as by what it did: the solicitor general conceded sincerity outright and then offered no iota of evidence on least intrusive means beyond the two documents establishing that very sincerity.

Justice Carpio closed his Dissent with a warning that the ruling could turn every religion into a separate republic, and voted for a suspension that would be lifted the moment Escritor manifested she had stopped cohabiting with Quilapio.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 25 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Estrada v. Escritor, in which the Court held that a court interpreter who lived with a man not her husband was not administratively liable, because she had made out a case for exemption based on her fundamental right to freedom of religion. Alejandro Estrada had asked the presiding judge of a Las Pinas trial court to investigate Soledad Escritor for an act he believed tarnished the image of the court, and she was charged with 'disgraceful and immoral conduct' under the Revised Administrative Code. Escritor testified that she had been widowed in 1998, that her arrangement with Luciano Quilapio Jr. had begun more than twenty years earlier while her own husband was living with another woman, and that as a member of Jehovah's Witnesses she had executed a 'Declaration of Pledging Faithfulness' approved by the elders and recorded in the Watch Tower Central Office, which made the union moral and binding within the congregation until legal impediments were lifted. An earlier Decision of August 4, 2003, which became the law of the case, had remanded the matter and ordered the solicitor general to intervene, and had settled that benevolent neutrality or accommodation was the framework for construing the religion clauses while the compelling-state-interest test governed the Free Exercise plea. The Court revisited the two opposing strains in American jurisprudence -- strict separation anchored on the Jeffersonian 'wall of separation' and benevolent neutrality -- and the Sherbert, Yoder and Smith line, distinguished mandatory, permissive and prohibited accommodation, and concluded that the Philippine Constitution gives accommodation more leeway, that criminal laws are not beyond the Free Exercise Clause, that accommodation protects minority religions from majoritarianism, and that the religion clauses are stated in absolute terms. Applying the three-step test, it noted that the solicitor general had conceded sincerity and centrality, shifting the burden to the government, which offered no evidence of paramount interests endangered and none at all on least intrusive means. Justice Carpio dissented, joined by the Chief Justice and Justices Morales and Callejo, arguing that Smith had overturned the Sherbert test and warning that 'today concubinage, tomorrow bigamy' would escape sanction; Justice Ynares-Santiago dissented separately, holding the issue legal rather than religious.
